subtype: Approach: asking an expert about the right food [Action]
passage: Yesterday I took my puppy for her first check. I asked Dr Tanvir, "What should I feed her?" Dr Tanvir said puppy food is best, that anything with chocolate or leftover curry is not safe for her, and to ask before adding anything new. At home I sat with Mama and Papa and we wrote a meal plan on a card, with the two unsafe foods in red. Then I stuck it inside the kitchen cupboard. My puppy sniffed the card, which made everyone laugh. I have never seen Papa read a card so seriously. - Amandeep

qa.q: Which foods did the vet say are not safe for the puppy?
qa.a: The vet said chocolate and leftover curry are not safe for the puppy.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when the puppy sniffed the card?
qa.a: Happy and amused, sharing a laugh with the family.

qa.q: What else could Amandeep ask the vet next time, and why?
qa.a: Amandeep could ask what changes as the puppy grows, so the meal plan can be updated with the vet's help.

qa.q: How might Mama and Papa see Amandeep's meal plan?
qa.a: They are probably pleased that Amandeep asked an expert first, and they join in the plan seriously.

grounding: A child asks the vet what to feed a puppy, learns that chocolate and spicy leftovers are unsafe, and makes a meal plan with the parents.

subtype: Approach: asking an expert about the right food [Action]
passage:
Clinic note, Saturday.
Sachin, who looks about ten, came in with his parents and a six-week-old puppy. Before I could start the check-up, he pulled out a folded paper and asked, "What can she eat? Can she have chocolate? Our leftovers?" I explained that chocolate is unsafe for dogs and that spicy, oily leftovers can upset her stomach. He wrote each thing down, spelling "chocolate" very carefully. I suggested puppy food, and plain rice with a little boiled chicken as a treat, and his mother asked about timings. While his parents paid, Sachin was already drawing a table: morning, afternoon, night, with a name beside each. I have given the family our feeding handout.
Ankita, veterinary clinic

qa.q: What did Sachin pull out before the check-up?
qa.a: A folded paper with his questions.

qa.q: What does Sachin spelling 'chocolate' carefully suggest?
qa.a: He felt serious and responsible, eager to get the puppy's food right.

qa.q: What else could Sachin do when unsure about a new food later?
qa.a: Check the clinic's handout or ask the vet before giving it, rather than guessing.

qa.q: How might Sachin's parents benefit from his table?
qa.a: The whole family can see who feeds the puppy when, so the meals stay regular and safe.

grounding: A vet's note records a boy asking what his puppy can safely eat and planning its meals with his parents.

subtype: Approach: asking an expert about the right food [Action]
passage:
Wednesday
Today the vet came to the free animal camp on our school field, and I carried Tora there in my arms. Last week Jaya fed her a bit of birthday cake with chocolate icing, and Tora was sick all night. At home we give her whatever is left from dinner, even fish curry with chillies. The vet said chocolate is not safe for dogs at all, and spicy leftovers can hurt their stomachs. I felt bad about the curry. At home I sat with Ma and Deuta and made a meal plan on the back of an old calendar: puppy food morning and evening, a little plain rice and boiled egg sometimes, NO chocolate, NO chilli. Jaya drew a crossed-out cake at the bottom.
Bhupen

qa.q: What did Jaya feed Tora last week?
qa.a: A bit of birthday cake with chocolate icing.

qa.q: How did Bhupen feel after the vet spoke?
qa.a: Bhupen felt bad, guilty about the spicy curry they had been giving Tora.

qa.q: What else could the family do to keep Tora safe?
qa.a: Keep chocolate and spicy food out of Tora's reach and tell visitors about the plan too.
Jaya may feel guilty about the cake, but joins in by drawing the crossed-out cake on the plan.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child asking a vet about safe food for a puppy and making a meal plan with the parents.
